# Introduction

John Mount of Win-Vector LLC posted a very interesting example of tide
prediction using known theory generating frequencies to model tides vs.
alternative methods of generated frequencies and prediction thereof. Please
give the post a full read to familiarize yourself with the problem:

<http://www.win-vector.com/blog/2019/08/lord-kelvin-data-scientist/>

# Predict Tides Using `NNS`

This is an excellent application of the time-series forecasting method in the
`NNS` R-package.

## Step 1: Install the Latest Version of `NNS`

```{r packages}
#library(devtools); install_github('OVVO-Financial/NNS', ref = "NNS-Beta-Version")
library(NNS)
packageVersion("NNS")
```

## Step 2: Read & Load the Variables, Create Train and Test Sets

The data are the Win-Vector `tides.RDS` file
(<https://github.com/WinVector/Examples/blob/master/Tides/tides.RDS>): water
levels at six-minute intervals from 2017-01-01. The download is checked
against the version this page was built from.

```{r data}
tides_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "tides.RDS")
if (!file.exists(tides_file)) {
  download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WinVector/Examples/master/Tides/tides.RDS",
                tides_file, mode = "wb")
}
stopifnot(unname(tools::md5sum(tides_file)) == "f7950d1c7e7fa31d6df0738ddf98bed3")
tides <- readRDS(tides_file)
```

Create the training set `dtrain` and the test set `dtest` using the dates
provided in the original post. The forecast origin is the cut date: nothing
after it is used for fitting or tuning.

```{r split}
base_date_time =  as.POSIXct('2001/01/01 00:00', tz = "UTC")
first_date_time =  as.POSIXct('2019/06/01 00:00', tz = "UTC")
cut_date_time = as.POSIXct('2019/07/15 00:00', tz = "UTC")

dtrain <- tides[tides$dt < cut_date_time, , drop = FALSE]
dtest <- tides[tides$dt >= cut_date_time, , drop = FALSE]

training_length <- dim(dtrain)[1] - dim(dtest)[1]

data.frame(set = c("dtrain", "dtest"),
           rows = c(nrow(dtrain), nrow(dtest)),
           from = c(min(dtrain$dt), min(dtest$dt)),
           to = c(max(dtrain$dt), max(dtest$dt)))
```

`NNS.ARMA.optim` tunes on the last `nrow(dtest)` observations of `dtrain`
(training set `r training_length` observations) and then forecasts the test
period from the whole training series.

## Step 3: Determine Frequencies, Optimize & Forecast

### 3.1: Determine Frequencies

In this step we will ascertain the most relevant periods via the `NNS.seas()`
function. To isolate just the periods, we call `nns_periods$periods`.

```{r seas}
nns_start.time <- Sys.time()
nns_periods <- NNS.seas(dtrain$tide_feet, modulo = 240, mod.only = FALSE)$periods
```

```{r seas-head}
head(nns_periods)

# Total relevant periods...
length(nns_periods)
```

### 3.2: Optimize the Combination of Frequencies

Now we will utilize the `nns_periods` in the `NNS.ARMA.optim` function, as
well as the number of forecast periods `h`.

***We are only going to use the first 200 relevant periods. There are
thousands more relevant periods that can be included but would require
additional computational resources.***

```{r optim}
nns_periods <- nns_periods[nns_periods < 44000]

arma_parameters <- NNS.ARMA.optim(variable = dtrain$tide_feet,
                                  h = nrow(dtest),
                                  training.set = length(dtrain$tide_feet) - nrow(dtest),
                                  pred.int = .95,
                                  seasonal.factor = nns_periods[1:200],
                                  print.trace = FALSE)

Sys.time() - nns_start.time
```

### 3.3: Forecast

Finally, we will extract the `results` using these optimum parameters, already
provided in our `arma_parameters` object along with the other following
parameters for the `NNS.ARMA` forecast.

```{r forecast}
arma_parameters[1:6]

nns_estimates <- arma_parameters$results
```

## Step 4: Evaluate the Results

Let's see how we did. The R-squared^[See Hayfield and Racine
<https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/np/vignettes/np.pdf>] between
predicted and actual is the presented metric.

$$R^2 = \frac{[\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})(\hat{y_i} - \bar{y})]^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{y_i} - \bar{y})^2}$$

```{r r2}
(sum((nns_estimates - mean(dtest$tide_feet)) * (dtest$tide_feet - mean(dtest$tide_feet))) ^ 2) /
  (sum((dtest$tide_feet - mean(dtest$tide_feet)) ^ 2) * sum((nns_estimates - mean(dtest$tide_feet)) ^ 2))
```

```{r plots, message = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(aes(x = dt), data = dtest) +
  geom_line(aes(y = tide_feet), color = 'blue', alpha = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = nns_estimates), color = 'black', alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = arma_parameters$lower.pred.int), color = 'red', alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = arma_parameters$upper.pred.int), color = 'red', alpha = 0.25) +
  ggtitle("prediction (black) superimposed on actuals (blue) on test")

ggplot_data <- data.frame(cbind(nns_estimates, dtest, arma_parameters$lower.pred.int,
                                arma_parameters$upper.pred.int))

ggplot(aes(x = nns_estimates, y = tide_feet), data = ggplot_data) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  ggtitle("prediction versus actual on test")
```

The red band is the optimizer's residual-quantile interval at the requested
95% level; its coverage of future values has not been assessed here.

## SCUM Forecasts and Timings

In addition to the `NNS` forecasts, the SCUM method (the median of ETS,
ARIMA, Theta and CES forecasts) was employed to generate forecasts and compare
timings. Theta stops with an error on this series, as it did in the original
run, and CES (`smooth::ces`) needs about 14 GB of memory here, so it runs only
when `run_ces <- TRUE` is set at the top of the source; the SCUM median uses
the forecasts that completed.

```{r scum-packages}
library(forecast)
library(smooth)
```

```{r scum}
# Start timing for SCUM
scum_start.time <- Sys.time()

# Generate SCUM forecasts
h <- length(dtest$tide_feet)

# Helper function for safe forecasting
safe_forecast <- function(forecast_function, data, h) {
  tryCatch({
    forecast_function(data, h = h)$mean
  }, error = function(e) {
    message(paste("Error in", deparse(substitute(forecast_function)), ":", e$message))
    return(rep(NA, h)) # Return NA for each horizon in case of an error
  })
}

# Perform individual forecasts safely
ets_forecast <- safe_forecast(function(data, h) forecast(ets(data), h = h), dtrain$tide_feet, h)
arima_forecast <- safe_forecast(function(data, h) forecast(auto.arima(data), h = h), dtrain$tide_feet, h)
theta_forecast <- safe_forecast(function(data, h) forecast(thetaf(data), h = h), dtrain$tide_feet, h)
ces_forecast <- if (run_ces) {
  safe_forecast(function(data, h) forecast(ces(data), h = h), dtrain$tide_feet, h)
} else rep(NA, h)

# Combine forecasts, excluding errors (NA)
forecasts_matrix <- rbind(ets_forecast, arima_forecast, theta_forecast, ces_forecast)
forecasts_matrix <- forecasts_matrix[complete.cases(forecasts_matrix), , drop = FALSE] # Remove rows with NA
scum_forecast <- apply(forecasts_matrix, 2, median)
rownames(forecasts_matrix)   # forecasts in the median

# End timing for SCUM
scum_end.time <- Sys.time()

# SCUM execution time
scum_end.time - scum_start.time
```

```{r scum-eval}
# SCUM evaluation
(sum((scum_forecast - mean(dtest$tide_feet)) * (dtest$tide_feet - mean(dtest$tide_feet))) ^ 2) /
  (sum((dtest$tide_feet - mean(dtest$tide_feet)) ^ 2) * sum((scum_forecast - mean(dtest$tide_feet)) ^ 2))

# Plot SCUM forecasts vs actual
ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = dtest$dt, y = dtest$tide_feet), color = 'blue', alpha = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(x = dtest$dt, y = scum_forecast), color = 'green', alpha = 0.7) +
  ggtitle("SCUM Forecasts vs Actual")
```

# Comments

The `NNS` method produces a very good result without any knowledge of or
access to the tide machine, and is well above the R-squared of 0.81 obtained
with FFT frequencies used in the Elastic Net Regularized Linear Regression in
the original blog post. Both are scored on the same test period after the same
cut date. Could `NNS` perform better? Yes. `NNS.ARMA` and `NNS.ARMA.optim` is
an active area of development.

Furthermore, more relevant periods and more granular data than the 6-minute
intervals would also help. How much better could `NNS` perform is an open
question...

`NNS` is not a one-trick pony: it is also applied to nonlinear continuous
regression, classification and econometric problems. See the following
examples:

- `NNS` Forecasting Presentation: <https://ssrn.com/abstract=3382300>
- `NNS` Forecasting vs. KERAS LSTM Deep Learning:
  <https://ovvo-financial.github.io/NNS/examples/Sunspots_example.html>
- Classification Using NNS Clustering Analysis: <https://ssrn.com/abstract=2864711>
- The 7 Reasons Most Econometric Investments Fail - NNS Contributions Towards
  Solutions: <https://ovvo-financial.github.io/NNS/examples/7_Econometric_Reasons.html>

I look forward to further discussions and collaboration with those equally as
passionate about these issues, and open to embracing alternative solutions. If
you found this presentation interesting or useful, please feel free to reach
out via e-mail: <ovvo.financial.systems@gmail.com>

Thanks for your interest!
